name: Jwala Narasimha Temple, Ahobilam
deity: Vishnu as Jwala Narasimha — the eight-armed, blazing form that destroys Hiranyakashipu
period: One of the Nava Narasimha shrines of Ahobilam in the Nallamala hills of Andhra Pradesh
style: Hill shrine built against the living rock
summary: High on the Achalachaya Meru above Upper Ahobilam, Jwala Narasimha shows the Lord at the fiery climax of his story — the eight-armed form that ends Hiranyakashipu's tyranny — beneath a ledge of rock.

sections.history: Jwala Narasimha is the highest of the Nava Narasimha, the nine shrines of Narasimha that pilgrims trace through the Nallamala hills of Ahobilam in Nandyal district. Tradition counts it as the very spot where the Lord's wrath blazed brightest — jwala means flame — at the moment he destroyed Hiranyakashipu. The shrine stands on the hill called Achalachaya Meru, about four kilometres of climbing beyond the Upper Ahobilam temple, close to the gorge through which the Bhavanasini stream falls. It is cared for within the Ahobila Matha's worship of the nine forms, and its stone fabric is generally associated with the Vijayanagara centuries, when Ahobilam drew sustained royal patronage.
sections.architecture: The shrine is modest: a small pillared hall built against a natural overhang of rock, with the sanctum tucked into the cliff so that the mountain itself forms its roof. The image is the arresting part — an eight-armed Narasimha holding Hiranyakashipu across his lap and tearing him open, while his other arms bear the conch and discus. Below the shrine lies a small pool that tradition calls the Raktakundam.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that after slaying Hiranyakashipu the Lord washed his blood-stained hands in the little pool below the shrine, and tradition holds that its water still carries a reddish tinge. The Ugra Stambham, the split crag pointed out as the pillar from which Narasimha burst forth, rises on the ridge above, so the climb to Jwala brings the pilgrim close to the heart of the Ahobilam story. In the astrological reading of the nine shrines, Jwala is linked with Mars.
sections.festivals: Narasimha Jayanti, in the month of Vaishakha, is the great day for all nine shrines, and the annual Brahmotsavam of Ahobilam draws pilgrims up to the hill temples. Swati, the Lord's birth star, is marked with special worship. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Jwala Narasimha is earned on foot. The path from Upper Ahobilam climbs steeply over rock and steps, passing Varaha Narasimha and crossing near the Bhavanasini falls; stretches are slippery after rain. Start early, carry water, and allow most of a morning for the round trip. Many pilgrims pause at the falls before the final ascent.

visit.timings: Worship is offered daily, but the shrine is reached only on foot and should be visited in daylight; set out well before midday. Confirm current timings locally, especially in the monsoon.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Reach Lower Ahobilam by road via Allagadda (Nandyal is the nearest major railhead), then take local transport up to Upper Ahobilam. From there a steep trail of about four kilometres leads to the shrine; local guides are available.
